title: Like a lotus in water
hook: the God-conscious one lives untouched, like a lotus in water

segments.voice: Yesterday, brahm giaanee: true in mind, true in speech, seeing the One in all. Your line was the god-conscious one. Today, the portrait gets its first picture.

If you've ever seen a lotus up close, you'll know the trick. It grows from the mud at the bottom of a pond. Its stem rises through murky water. Then the leaf and the flower open on the surface, and if you splash water on them, it beads up and rolls right off. The leaf is in the water its whole life, and it doesn't get wet. The Guru Granth Sahib returns to this flower more than once. Today it opens the first stanza of the brahm giaanee's portrait.
screen: `ROOTED IN MUD.` → `RISING THROUGH MURKY WATER.` → `THE WATER BEADS AND ROLLS OFF.`

segments.voice: The first line: brahm giaanee sadaa nirlep. The God-conscious one is always nirlep, untouched, unstained. Lep is a coating, something that sticks to you; nir means without. So: nothing sticks. Then the picture: jaise jal meh kamal alep. Just as the lotus in water stays unstained. Kamal is the lotus. Notice what the picture doesn't say. The lotus doesn't leave the pond or float off to some clean place. It lives in the water, all its life. That matters in Sikh teaching, which asks people to live in the world, work, marry, raise children, pay bills, and not run away to the forest. Guru Nanak used the same image in the Sidh Gosht, when yogis asked how one crosses the ocean of the world: like a lotus in water, untouched, and like a duck swimming in a stream, whose feathers stay dry. The brahm giaanee is in the mess. The mess just doesn't stick. The next line adds a second picture: the God-conscious one is free of fault, like the sun that dries up everything. The sun shines on clean and dirty places alike and doesn't get dirty doing it. Two pictures, one idea: you can be fully in the middle of things, the office, the family argument, the crowded train, and still not be stained. Untouched doesn't mean unfeeling. It means the anger in the room doesn't become your anger.
screen: `NIRLEP: NOTHING STICKS.` · `KAMAL: THE LOTUS STAYS IN THE POND.` · `GURU NANAK: THE LOTUS AND THE DUCK.` · `THE SUN, UNSTAINED BY WHAT IT DRIES.` · then, large: `UNTOUCHED, LIKE THE LOTUS.`

segments.voice: Think of a small mess waiting for you today, an inbox, a difficult relative, a sink full of dishes, and picture yourself in the middle of it; then picture a lotus leaf, the water beading up and rolling off. Breathe in: I'm in the water. Breathe out: it rolls off; you're not pretending the mess isn't there, only not letting it soak in.
Kamal, the lotus. The God-conscious one lives in the world, untouched, like the kamal in the pond.
Your line: untouched, like the lotus. In the pond all its life, and still dry. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs often use the lotus in water, from Sukhmani Sahib and Guru Nanak's Sidh Gosht, to describe living as a householder in the world without being stained by it.

what a scholar hears: nirlep (nir- 'without' + lep 'coating'); the lotus image recurs in Gurbani, notably in Guru Nanak's Sidh Gosht (Ang 938), as the model of the householder's detachment.

chat.says: If Sikhs want to stay pure, why not leave the busy world and live somewhere quiet?
options: Like the lotus: it lives in the pond all its life and stays dry. You can be in the world, unstained.
Untouched means unfeeling: the stanza says to stop caring about the people around you.
The lotus picture says to stay in the world only until you're ready to leave it.
chat.meaning: Brahm giaanee sadaa nirlep: like the lotus in water, the God-conscious one lives in the world, and nothing sticks.
